title: Oxmiq Labs HBF in AI Compute at Hot Chips 2026
gist: Oxmiq Labs' Hot Chips 2026 presentation frames high-bandwidth flash (HBF) not as cheap HBM but as a narrow capacity tool for AI inference — winning only in specific regimes like small-batch MoE serving and long-context sparse-attention KV cache, while HBM still dominates at rack scale.

insights.claim: Oxmiq Labs' HBF hardware spec spans three grades with maximum user bandwidth rising from 0.384 TB/s to 3.072 TB/s and UCIe rates climbing from 8 GT/s to 32 GT/s, with capacity topping out at 512 GiB on a 16-high stack.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Concrete spec ladder for a nascent memory tier competing for AI accelerator BOM dollars; useful baseline for tracking HBF product announcements against vendor claims.
insights.locator: Oxmiq opens by laying out the HBF hardware specification across three grades.

insights.claim: Oxmiq's core sales pitch is that HBF delivers 8 to 16 times the capacity of HBM at the same cost.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Headline capacity-per-dollar claim that HBF vendors will use to pitch memory suppliers and AI accelerator makers on adding an HBF tier.
insights.quote: This pitch is that HBF delivers 8 to 16 times the capacity of HBM at the same cost.
insights.locator: Oxmiq opens by laying out the HBF hardware specification across three grades.

insights.claim: Oxmiq positions HBF using an alpha (bandwidth) and beta (cost) axis framework, arguing HBF occupies a distinct capacity point on that landscape rather than being simply a cheaper version of HBM.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: This alpha/beta framing is a mental model investors can reuse to evaluate future memory-tier announcements (HBM, HBF, CXL, etc.) by where they sit on cost vs. bandwidth rather than by marketing claims alone.
insights.quote: HBF is a capacity point on this landscape, not a cheaper version of HBM.
insights.locator: Oxmiq frames HBF within the memory technology landscape using alpha and beta.

insights.claim: Oxmiq argues the correct metric for evaluating AI inference memory isn't dollars-per-gigabyte but the cost of serving a token, defined by 'hold' (capacity) and 'feed' (bandwidth) requirements.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Reframes how buyers of AI inference hardware should benchmark memory options — capacity/cost comparisons alone are misleading without factoring bandwidth-per-token needs.
insights.quote: the real metric is the cost of serving the token in terms of hold and feed (bandwidth)
insights.locator: Oxmiq is now breaking down the cost of serving in terms of a token.

insights.claim: Large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models open up a 'small batch capacity sub-phase' where the full model can be held in memory with lower bandwidth being acceptable, unlike dense models which need bandwidth scaled to batch size and tokens/s.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Identifies MoE serving specifically (not dense LLMs generally) as the workload segment where a capacity-over-bandwidth memory tier like HBF has genuine product-market fit.
insights.locator: Next comes model personality, with a larger MoE model set against dense models.

insights.claim: Across three same-cost deployment configs (HBM-only baseline, all-HBF, and a 2x HBF/6x HBM mix), peak bandwidth drops from 22 TB/s (HBM baseline) to 12.8 TB/s (all-HBF) while capacity rises from 288 GB to 4 TB.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Quantifies the direct bandwidth-for-capacity trade at constant cost, giving a concrete reference point for evaluating future HBF-equipped accelerator SKUs.
insights.locator: Oxmiq lays out a few ways to deploy HBF, covering an HBM-only baseline, an all-HBF configuration, and a 2x HBF-6x HBM mix.

insights.claim: In a short-context (256x256) scenario, an all-HBF system wins on cost at low batch sizes but suffers 85 percent 'dead capacity' — memory that sits unused.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Shows HBF's capacity advantage can be largely wasted in short-context workloads, limiting its addressable use case to specific inference profiles rather than general deployment.
insights.quote: HBF wins on cost at low batch, but with 85 percent “dead capacity.”
insights.locator: First, Oxmiq examines an all-HBF system with a short 256-by-256 context.

insights.claim: At long context (1M tokens in, 1K out), HBF's capacity advantage holds only while bandwidth demand stays low; beyond that threshold HBM becomes the better option.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Sets a practical crossover rule for system architects: HBF is favorable only up to a bandwidth-demand ceiling, after which HBM should be used instead.
insights.locator: Moving to long context at 1M tokens in and 1K out, the picture shifts.

insights.claim: Using HBM as a hot-expert cache alongside HBF only pays off at low batch sizes or when similar queries are batched together, because expert popularity flattens out across mixed query workloads.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Caching strategies for MoE expert weights are workload-dependent, not a universal win — relevant for anyone designing or evaluating inference serving stacks.
insights.locator: The next case considers a mixed case in which HBM acts as a hot-expert cache.

insights.claim: In a 72-GPU rack simulation running a decode-centric Kimi-K2 1T-parameter model at FP4 with 1M tokens in and 1K out, HBF delivers roughly 14x the capacity for about 0.6x the bandwidth versus the HBM baseline at the same rack cost.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Headline capacity/bandwidth tradeoff figure for trillion-parameter MoE inference at rack scale — a concrete number for evaluating HBF's real-world value proposition against HBM-only racks.
insights.quote: HBF buys roughly 14x the capacity for about 0.6x the bandwidth
insights.locator: Oxmiq details its system and simulation setup at the rack level across a 72-GPU rack.

insights.claim: Oxmiq's simulation shows cheaper dollars-per-gigabyte does not translate into cheaper dollars-per-token, and that HBM keeps its cost edge at rack scale while HBF fits best where the goal is capacity per box rather than throughput.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Directly undercuts a naive HBF bull case built on raw $/GB savings — investors evaluating HBF/NAND suppliers should model $/token at deployment scale, not sticker price per gigabyte.
insights.quote: Cheaper dollars per GB does not equal cheaper dollars per token.
insights.locator: A first sim check plots rack dollars per token against single-server capacity.

insights.claim: HBF access happens in 64 KB chunks for maximum bandwidth, retains data for roughly 24 hours while powered on at 85 degrees Celsius, and requires host-managed lifecycle handling — since it is read-optimized and write-constrained, memory placement becomes a software engineering problem rather than a pure hardware swap.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: HBF adoption requires new memory-allocator and placement software before it's production-usable — a gating factor for how fast this technology could actually ship in real inference stacks.
insights.quote: roughly 24 hours of power-on data retention at 85 degrees Celsius and host-managed lifecycle handling
insights.locator: Oxmiq then turns to the software constraints of HBF.

insights.claim: In a model like Kimi-K3, roughly 93 percent of bytes (1.45 TB) are MoE expert weights, leading Oxmiq to argue HBF should hold the MoE expert pool and KV-cache offload while HBM handles attention weights and other hot data.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete data-driven rationale for a hybrid HBM+HBF memory architecture tailored to where bytes actually live in large MoE models.
insights.quote: Roughly 93 percent of bytes are MoE expert weights at 1.45 TB
insights.locator: Oxmiq then looks at where the memory actually goes in a model like Kimi-K3.

insights.claim: Oxmiq treats vLLM as the production-default inference engine and primary integration target for HBF, over alternatives like SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, and AWS Neuron.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Signals where HBF software tooling and plugins will likely appear first — vLLM ecosystem watchers should expect HBF-related integration work there before other serving stacks.
insights.locator: The company walks through the inference engine ecosystem.

insights.claim: Oxmiq proposes a vLLM plugin that uses HBF in place of host CPU pinned memory for the KV cache and MoE expert pools; a GPU configured with 4x HBM and 4x HBF stacks would reach 2.2 TB of capacity at about 17.4 TB/s of peak bandwidth, far beyond today's CPU-offload paths.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Concrete proposed hardware/software configuration that could materially raise achievable memory capacity per GPU if implemented — a specific product concept to track for adoption signals.
insights.locator: Inside vLLM, Oxmiq proposes a plugin that uses HBF in place of host CPU pinned memory.

insights.claim: Sparse-attention model architectures such as DeepSeek Sparse Attention and Compressed Sparse Attention are a genuine fit for HBF's low-bandwidth, high-capacity zone, though this benefit is conditional on models adopting that architecture style.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Ties HBF's commercial prospects to the broader adoption trajectory of sparse-attention model architectures — a variable worth tracking alongside model-architecture trends.
insights.locator: Oxmiq sees attention sparsity as a genuine HBF fit.

insights.claim: Cheap HBF capacity could reduce the number of expert-parallel (EP) shards needed for MoE serving, letting as few as 2 nodes hold experts locally in HBF instead of sharding across 8 GPUs and incurring all-to-all communication traffic at every layer.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: If realized, this could reduce networking/interconnect overhead in large MoE inference clusters, a potential secondary effect on demand for high-bandwidth interconnect/networking gear in AI datacenters.
insights.locator: Oxmiq closes its case with expert parallelism.

insights.claim: Oxmiq's own conclusion is notably narrower than typical HBF/NAND vendor messaging: HBF wins only in specific regimes such as MoE serving at small batch and long-context sparse KV-cache workloads, not as a general HBM replacement.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Tempers the bullish HBF narrative being pushed by memory/NAND vendors; investors should treat HBF as a niche inference tool, not a broad HBM disruptor, when assessing memory-sector capex or supplier claims.
insights.quote: HBF wins only where bandwidth demand is low, such as MoE with small batch and long-context sparse KV.
insights.locator: Oxmiq wraps with a set of takeaways.

insights.claim: The author views Oxmiq's candid, narrowly-scoped framing of HBF's use cases as unusually balanced compared to other, less balanced HBF promoters in the industry.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Signals to readers that most HBF marketing in the industry currently overstates the technology's applicability, making Oxmiq's talk a useful reality-check reference point.
insights.quote: Those observations are an interesting framing, to say the least, especially compared to many HBF promoters, who are less balanced in their messaging.
insights.locator: Those observations are an interesting framing, to say the least.

insights.claim: The author concludes HBF is best understood as a capacity instrument for a narrow but real slice of inference work, particularly large MoE models where expert weights dominate memory footprint, and that an HBF-aware memory allocator and placement policy are the missing pieces before it becomes practical to deploy.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Frames the near-term bottleneck for HBF commercialization as a software/systems problem (memory placement/allocation), not a hardware manufacturing problem — relevant for timing any investment thesis around HBF suppliers.
insights.quote: HBF looks like a capacity instrument aimed at a narrow but real slice of inference work, particularly large MoE models where expert weights dominate.
insights.locator: Final Words
